notes.h: Finance needed to buy a home (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Few buyers can pay for a home from savings alone, so most borrow. The amount a buyer must borrow is the purchase price minus the deposit, plus any costs of buying that the buyer cannot pay from savings.
points: The factors that determine the amount of finance required are the purchase price (which depends on the size, type and location of the house, and whether it is new or second-hand) and the buyer's own savings and deposit.
Additional costs of buying add to the total needed, so a buyer must budget for more than the price: solicitor's (legal) fees for the transfer of ownership, and stamp duty, a tax paid on the purchase.

Further costs are the valuation and survey carried out for the lender (to check what the house is worth and what condition it is in), an application or lender fee, land registry fees (to record the new owner), home insurance, and any fitting-out, furnishing or repair costs.

A deposit is the buyer's own money paid towards the purchase price. Lenders require a minimum percentage deposit, set by Central Bank rules, and supply the balance as a mortgage, so saving a deposit is a main barrier for first-time buyers.
A mortgage is a long-term loan to buy property, repaid with interest in regular (usually monthly) instalments over a term of many years. Interest is the cost of borrowing the money.
A mortgage is secured on the house itself, which means that if repayments are not made the lender can take possession of the property and sell it to recover the loan. This is called repossession.
notes.tip: If asked what a mortgage is, say that it is a loan secured on the property and give the consequence: the lender can repossess if repayments are missed.

notes.h: Sources of finance for buying a home (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A buyer usually combines several sources of money. Some are the buyer's own, some are borrowed from a lender, and some come from the State or family.
points: The buyer's own savings are the first source, and they make up the deposit that lenders require before they will lend the balance.
A mortgage from a bank or other lending institution is the main source of finance, because it provides the large sum that savings cannot cover.
A local authority home loan is government-backed and is for people who qualify but cannot get a commercial loan.
A credit union loan is usually a smaller amount, for example to help with a deposit or home improvements.
Help from parents or family, as a gift or a loan, is often used towards the deposit.

State supports for buyers include the First Home shared equity scheme (the State and participating lenders take a share in a new home, which the buyer can buy back), the Help to Buy incentive for first-time buyers of new homes, and affordable purchase schemes run by local authorities.
notes.tip: When asked to outline sources of finance, name the buyer's own savings and deposit, a lender, a local authority loan, a credit union and help from family, and say what each provides.

notes.h: Conditions attached to mortgage approval (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A lending institution assesses whether the applicant can repay the loan and whether the property is a suitable security for it. Each condition below protects the lender by making sure the loan can be repaid, or the property sold if it is not.
points: Borrowing limit: the loan is capped at a set multiple of the applicant's gross income (income before tax), so the borrower is not lent more than can be repaid. The multiple is set by Central Bank rules and changes.
Loan-to-value limit: the loan cannot exceed a set share of the property's value, so the buyer must provide the balance as a deposit. The rules differ for first-time buyers and others.
Secure, continuous employment: the applicant must be in stable work so that repayments can be met over the term. The self-employed supply accounts instead.
Proof of income: payslips, a P60 (the yearly summary of pay and tax), and tax and bank statements show the lender what the applicant earns.

Good financial record: a clean credit history with no missed repayments or unpaid debts, a record of regular saving and reasonable spending habits. Existing debts and commitments reduce the amount lent.
Term of the loan: repayments are spread over a long period, but an older applicant is usually offered a shorter term so the loan ends before retirement.

Property: the lender has it valued and surveyed, and it must be in good condition and good value as security. The lender checks the title deeds through a solicitor, and the buyer must have buildings insurance for the term.
Mortgage protection insurance, plus proof of identity and address so the lender can confirm who the borrower is.
notes.tip: This is the most frequently examined item in this subsection. Four conditions, each developed with the reason the lender wants it, earn more than eight conditions that are only named. Cover income, deposit, credit record, term and property.

notes.b: A mortgage is a large debt that may last decades, and the borrower could die before it is repaid. A mortgage protection policy is a life assurance policy that protects the lender's loan and the borrower's family if the borrower dies during the term.
points: Mortgage protection is a term life assurance policy for the length of the mortgage and the amount of the loan. Life assurance means premiums (regular payments) are made and a sum is paid out when the insured person dies.
If the borrower dies during the term, the insurer repays the outstanding mortgage balance to the lender, so the family keeps the home.
Without cover, the remaining debt would fall on the borrower's family, who could be forced to sell the home.
Life assurance in general can run for life, whereas mortgage protection runs for the term only, and the sum insured falls as the loan is repaid (a decreasing term policy).
Under the Consumer Credit Act 1995 a lender must make sure that the borrower has mortgage protection, with exceptions such as where cover cannot be obtained because of age or health.
The borrower may buy mortgage protection from the lender's group scheme, an insurer or a broker, and cannot be forced to buy it from the lender.
Mortgage protection does not pay the repayments if the borrower is ill, disabled or made redundant, because it pays only on death. Income protection is a separate policy.
Annuity and pension-linked mortgages require a mortgage protection policy to be taken out with the loan.
An endowment mortgage does not need a separate protection policy, because its life assurance policy already covers the loan.
notes.tip: To explain why mortgage protection is necessary, say that without it the family would lose the home or inherit the debt. Do not mix it up with home insurance, which covers the buildings and contents: the lender requires both.

notes.b: Mortgages differ in how the capital (the sum borrowed) and the interest are repaid. Annuity, endowment, pension-linked and tracker mortgages are the main types to be able to describe.
points: Annuity (repayment) mortgage: each repayment pays part of the interest and part of the capital borrowed, so the amount owed falls over time. Early repayments are mostly interest. It is the most common type, the rate may be fixed, variable or a combination, and it needs mortgage protection.

Endowment mortgage: the borrower pays only interest on the loan, plus a premium on a life assurance (endowment) policy designed to repay the loan when it matures. The policy yield may not fully cover the loan, and no separate protection policy is needed. It is no longer widely available.

Pension-linked mortgage: interest is paid on the loan and contributions are paid into a pension scheme, and the loan is repaid from the pension lump sum on retirement. It needs mortgage protection, is rare today, and was popular with self-employed people because of tax relief on pension contributions.

Tracker mortgage: the interest rate follows a published benchmark rate, the European Central Bank (ECB) rate, plus a fixed margin, so repayments rise and fall with the ECB rate. Trackers are no longer offered to new borrowers, but you may be asked to describe one.
Interest-only mortgage: the borrower pays only the interest for a period, so the capital is still owed at the end of that period. It is rarely offered.
Current account (offset) mortgage: savings held in a linked current account reduce the balance on which interest is charged. It is rarely offered.
Local authority mortgages and loans are also accepted as types of home finance.
notes.tip: When asked to name and describe one type of mortgage, give the name and then two or three points of description. Annuity is the safest choice: repayments of interest and capital, the balance falling, protection needed, and the rate options. Do not confuse endowment (a life policy repays the capital at maturity) with annuity (capital repaid steadily).

notes.h: Interest rates and repayments (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Interest is the cost of borrowing, so the rate on a mortgage decides how much the borrower pays each month and in total. A borrower can choose how the rate behaves and how long the loan lasts.
points: A fixed rate is set for an agreed period of a number of years, so repayments are the same during that period and the buyer is protected from rises. The buyer misses out if rates fall, and ending early may carry a charge.
A variable rate changes with the lender's rate, which tends to follow market and ECB rates, so repayments rise when rates rise and fall when rates fall. This means there is risk for the borrower.
A combination (split) mortgage divides the loan between a fixed portion and a variable portion.
A fixed rate is often higher than the variable rate at the start, because the lender takes on the risk of rate changes.
A longer loan term gives smaller repayments but more interest in total, because interest is charged for more years.
A shorter loan term means higher repayments but less interest paid in total.
notes.tip: For a question on one advantage of a fixed rate and of a variable rate, give the fixed rate's protection from rises and the variable rate's benefit when rates fall. Explain fixed and variable rates by saying what happens to the repayments.

keyTerms.definition: The part of the purchase price paid by the buyer from their own funds, with the lender providing the rest.
A loan to buy property, secured on the property, which the lender can repossess if repayments are not made.
A life assurance policy that pays off the outstanding mortgage if the borrower dies during the loan term.
A borrower's total income before tax and deductions, used by lenders to set the maximum loan.
A repayment mortgage in which each repayment covers interest and part of the capital, so the debt reduces over the term.
A mortgage in which the borrower pays interest on the loan and a premium on a life assurance policy that is intended to repay the loan at maturity.
A mortgage whose interest rate moves in line with a published benchmark rate, plus a fixed margin.
An interest rate that changes with market rates, so the borrower's repayments can rise or fall.
A credit agreement in which goods are paid for in instalments, with ownership passing only after the final payment.
The total yearly cost of credit, expressed as a percentage, which must be disclosed to the borrower.

factCards.definition: Fixed, variable and a combination of the two.

factCards.definition: Solicitor's and legal fees; stamp duty; the valuation and survey carried out for the lender.

questions.prompt: Explain what a tracker mortgage is and how its repayments change over the loan term.
questions.model: A tracker mortgage has an interest rate that follows a published benchmark rate, usually the European Central Bank rate, plus a fixed margin. When the benchmark rate rises, the interest rate and repayments rise; when it falls, they fall. The repayments therefore vary over the term, and the borrower carries the risk of rate increases.

questions.prompt: Discuss the conditions a lending institution is likely to set before approving a mortgage, and explain the purpose of a mortgage protection policy.
questions.model: Borrowing limit: the loan is set as a multiple of gross income. Loan-to-value: the loan is limited to a share of the property's value, so the buyer must provide a deposit. Secure employment and proof of income: payslips and a P60 show the applicant can meet repayments. Good credit history and regular saving show sound financial management. Term of the loan: long repayment periods, with shorter terms for older applicants. Property condition: the house is surveyed and must be in good condition as security. Mortgage protection policy: a life assurance policy that pays off the outstanding balance if the borrower dies during the term, so that the family is not left with the debt and the lender is repaid. It is required with annuity and pension-linked mortgages, while an endowment mortgage's life policy serves the same purpose.
